strategy:
1. Approach and rationale

Use a two-stage, derivative-free search: first solve a small convex semidefinite moment relaxation of the finite-dimensional minimax problem, then use its feasible mean and covariance to seed randomized rounding and a rank-weighted projected evolution strategy. Every candidate used as an answer is projected onto the capped simplex and ranked by the exact evaluator score.

The bottleneck is the maximum of 2n−1 nonconvex quadratic lag functions. The identity that a rank-one moment matrix represents all quadratic products exactly gives a convex relaxation that considers the lags jointly and can reveal correlated perturbation directions. Dropping the rank-one requirement makes the relaxation potentially loose; its mean and covariance are therefore search guidance, not a replacement objective or a returned solution. Randomized rounding and the evolution strategy explore feasible candidates without derivatives or an assumption that the active maximum lag stays fixed.

This is materially different from the supplied parent and the previous strategies: it does not use the parent’s per-lag linearization/proximity steps, a nonlinear epigraph SLSQP solve, a log-sum-exp projected-gradient trajectory, or pairwise coordinate-transfer polishing. Its primary search information comes from a moment SDP and its candidate updates come from a rank-selected population. Exact-score checks, the valid relaxation construction, and the fallback guarantee described below are mathematical or implementation facts. The hypothesis is that the relaxation’s covariance and population adaptation may expose useful basins that a local trajectory misses. Neither the relaxation nor this heuristic guarantees a score below 0.3808, improvement over the parent, or a global optimum. Preserve a feasible parent-derived fallback and never replace it with a worse exact-scored vector.

2. Mathematical specification

For runtime n, let h be a real vector of shape (n,), dx=2/n, and s=n/2. The discrete constraints are 0≤h[i]≤1 and sum(h)=s. This includes odd n, for which s is a half-integer.

For every integer lag d from −(n−1) through n−1, define p=max(d,0), q=max(−d,0), and m=n−|d|. The exact finite-support lag score is

r_d(h) = dx · sum over j=0,...,m−1 of h[p+j]·(1−h[q+j]).

The evaluator’s authoritative objective is C(h)=max_d r_d(h), computed as max(np.correlate(h, 1−h, mode='full')·dx). The full correlation has 2n−1 entries; it is linear, not circular. The overlap at a nonzero lag has only m terms. Do not replace that partial sum by the full mass or by a complement of an autocorrelation.

For the convex relaxation, introduce u in R^n, a symmetric matrix Y in R^(n×n), and scalar t. If u=h and Y=hhᵀ, the lifted moment matrix M=[[1,uᵀ],[u,Y]]= [1;u][1;u]ᵀ is positive semidefinite and every lag is exactly

r_d = dx · (sum from i=p to p+m−1 of u[i] − sum from j=0 to m−1 of Y[p+j,q+j]).

Form the SDP by minimizing t subject to 0≤u≤1, sum(u)=s, t≥0, M⪰0, Y·1=s·u, and, for every i,j, the valid product-envelope constraints 0≤Y[i,j], Y[i,j]≥u[i]+u[j]−1, Y[i,j]≤u[i], and Y[i,j]≤u[j]. For every lag impose the affine constraint r_d(u,Y)≤t. The row equality follows from Y=uuᵀ and sum(u)=s; it is a valid strengthening of the relaxation. All these constraints are affine or positive-semidefinite constraints, so this is a convex SDP. It contains every original feasible rank-one lift, but it also admits non-rank-one points; its minimum is only a relaxation bound and must not be reported as C(h).

For a solver result (u,Y), the Schur complement of M gives S=Y−uuᵀ⪰0 in exact arithmetic. Also S·1=0 from the row equality. Symmetrize S, project it onto the sum-zero subspace to remove numerical error, and clip negative eigenvalues to zero. Use u plus scaled samples from this covariance as proposals; project every proposal back onto the capped simplex. This is heuristic rounding, not an assertion that the sampled vector realizes Y. The original C(h), evaluated from np.correlate, judges every candidate and the returned solution.

3. Implementation procedure

3.1. Define run(seed=42, **kwargs) and all helpers as top-level functions. Use NumPy and optionally CVXPY; CVXPY may be imported in a guarded top-level try/except so its absence disables only the SDP stage. No helper may be nested or be a lambda. Run serially on the single allowed CPU. Do not use filesystem or network I/O, parallel workers, or any unlisted library. Do not redefine, serialize, or hard-code initial_h_values; read the pre-imported array at runtime without mutating it.

3.2. Resolve n and create the fallback inside run. Attempt to read initial_h_values as a float64 one-dimensional array using a separate working copy. If its flattened size is in [1,999], that size takes precedence over kwargs['n_points'], even if the values prove unusable. Otherwise accept kwargs['n_points'] only when it converts to a finite integer in [1,999]; use n=47 if it does not. Do not change resolution during the run, so no interpolation is required.

If a parent of length n is finite and all entries lie in [−1e−8,1+1e−8], make its feasible parent-derived fallback with project_capped. This repairs mass jointly and handles only tiny box excursions; never mutate the supplied array. If it is absent, nonfinite, materially outside the box, or projection fails, use h[i]=0.5 for every i. The constant vector is feasible for every allowed n. Save a copy and its exact score before search. In particular, for n=1 the only feasible vector is [0.5], so return the fallback immediately. Convert seed to an integer for np.random.default_rng; if conversion or generator creation fails, use seed 42. Use this one generator for all random operations.

3.3. Implement top-level project_capped(z,n), returning a float64 vector or failure, and is_feasible(h,n). Projection must jointly enforce bounds and mass. Reject a wrong shape or nonfinite z, then clip finite extreme proposal values to [−1e6,1e6]. The Euclidean capped-simplex projection has h[i]=clip(z[i]−lambda,0,1), with lambda chosen so sum(h)=s. Set lo=min(z)−1 and hi=max(z); these bracket an all-ones and an all-zeros clipped vector. Do 80 bisection steps. At a midpoint, if the clipped sum exceeds s, move lo to the midpoint; otherwise move hi to it. Construct h using the final midpoint.

Correct the remaining floating-point residual s−sum(h) by walking over coordinates and adding no more than 1−h[i] for a positive residual, or subtracting no more than h[i] for a negative residual. Recompute and repeat a pass if necessary. This correction preserves the box; do not clip and rescale successively. Reject nonfinite output, any bound violation beyond 1e−12, or final absolute mass error above 1e−9. is_feasible requires shape (n,), finite entries, bounds within 1e−12, and absolute mass error at most 1e−9. All proposals must pass it after projection.

3.4. Implement exact_score(h,n). Return positive infinity for an infeasible vector, a nonfinite correlation, or an exception. Otherwise calculate dx=2.0/n and the full array np.correlate(h, 1.0−h, mode='full')*dx, check every entry is finite, and return its maximum as a Python float. This exact helper is authoritative for the parent score, pool scores, evolutionary ranking, candidate archive, fallback comparison, and final return. Do not use the SDP t value or any approximate objective as a score.

3.5. Implement solve_moment_relaxation(n), returning a finite raw u vector and covariance S or failure. Run it only for 2≤n≤64; larger dense lifts are deliberately skipped. Build the model in section 2 with h as an n-by-1 CVXPY variable, symmetric Y, and scalar t. Build M with cp.bmat([[one, h.T],[h,Y]]) and impose M >> 0. The McCormick matrix inequalities can be expressed elementwise using h times an all-ones row or column: Y≥0, Y≥h·1ᵀ+1·hᵀ−1, Y≤h·1ᵀ, and Y≤1·hᵀ. Impose Y·1=s·h. For each d, add dx·(sum(h[p:p+m])−trace(Y[p:p+m,q:q+m]))≤t. Do not add Y=hhᵀ or claim the SDP solves the nonconvex problem.

Only attempt installed SDP-capable solvers: MOSEK first and CVXOPT second, checking cp.installed_solvers(). Do not send this PSD model to CBC, GLOP, GLPK, GUROBI, PDLP, SCIP, XPRESS, or ECOS. Use verbose=False; for CVXOPT use a finite cap such as max_iters=80 with abstol, reltol, and feastol of 1e−7. If MOSEK is used, request one thread and a modest solver time cap if supported. Catch import, canonicalization, license, solver, and status errors and try the next supported solver or skip the relaxation. Accept only optimal or optimal_inaccurate status with finite u, Y, and t values of the expected shapes. The t value is only a solver-result validity check.

For accepted values, retain raw u for covariance construction and also pass it through project_capped when adding its mean as a candidate. Form S=Y−uuᵀ, symmetrize, and apply P S P where P=I−11ᵀ/n. If covariance construction or eigendecomposition fails or is nonfinite, retain the feasible mean candidate but report no usable covariance. Otherwise use eigh, replace negative eigenvalues by zero, and cap exceptionally large eigenvalues at n before sampling. The PSD relaxation’s candidate mean and covariance must still be validated and exact-scored like any other proposal.

3.6. Build a deduplicated feasible start pool using a top-level helper that projects each proposal, checks is_feasible, computes exact_score, and appends it only if its maximum absolute coordinate difference from every stored start is at least 1e−8. Add the saved fallback first and never remove it. Then propose, in order, the fallback reversal, its complement, the reversal of that complement, the constant 0.5 vector, a block vector, an alternating vector, a cosine vector, two Gaussian perturbations of the fallback, and a seeded uniform vector. For the block vector set the first floor(n/2) entries to one and, if n is odd, the next entry to 0.5; set the rest to zero. For the alternating vector use one at even indices and zero at odd indices before projection. For the cosine use 0.5+0.45·cos(2πi/P), i=0,...,n−1, with P=max(2,n/3). Use Gaussian standard deviations 0.04 and 0.12. Reversal and complement preserve the exact maximum over all lags for feasible inputs, but are included to offer different search geometries, not as claimed improvements.

If the SDP supplies u and usable S, also add the projected mean and 12 randomized-rounding proposals. With S=Q diag(a) Qᵀ, form raw proposals u+gamma·Q·sqrt(max(a,0))·xi, where xi has independent standard-normal entries from the seeded generator and gamma cycles through 0.5, 1.0, and 1.5. Project and exact-score each. Cap the pool at 32 unique starts, preserving insertion order and the fallback. If the relaxation is unavailable, all non-SDP starts remain usable.

3.7. Implement a top-level projected rank-weighted evolution routine; do not use gradients, SLSQP, or a relaxed score in its selection. Initialize its mean mu from a feasible pool candidate and calculate its exact score. For n≤64, initialize a covariance shape A from P S P if S is usable, otherwise from P. Symmetrize, take the positive-semidefinite part by eigenvalue clipping, normalize trace to n−1, blend 85% of this normalized matrix with 15% of P, and normalize again. For n>64 use a diagonal variance vector initially equal to ones; this avoids dense covariance storage at high resolutions.

For each generation include mu as a population member, then generate lambda offspring. For n≤64 sample noise Q·sqrt(max(eigenvalues(A),0))·xi using eigh(A); for n>64 sample sqrt(variance) elementwise times xi. For each child set z=mu+sigma·noise, project z with project_capped, require feasibility, and score it with exact_score. If a numerical factorization fails, use a seeded standard-normal vector with its mean removed for that draw. A failed proposal is discarded or assigned infinite score; it cannot enter the archive.

Rank the center and offspring by their exact scores. Let q=max(2,floor((lambda+1)/4)), capped at the population size. For ranks j=0,...,q−1 assign weight q−j and normalize the weights to sum to one. Set the next mean to the weighted vector average of those q feasible elites and pass it through project_capped to correct roundoff. This mean remains feasible in exact arithmetic because the capped simplex is convex. Update the run’s best archive only when a feasible candidate’s exact score is lower by more than 1e−12; the mean is also exact-scored before it can update the archive.

Adapt the shape using the same elites. For n≤64 calculate E=sum_j w[j]·(x[j]−mu_new)(x[j]−mu_new)ᵀ/max(sigma²,1e−8), project E to P E P, and if its trace is positive normalize it to trace n−1. Set A to the symmetric normalized blend 0.8 A+0.2 E, with a small 1e−4 P ridge before final trace normalization. If E is invalid or has negligible trace, retain A. For n>64 calculate each coordinate’s weighted elite squared deviation divided by max(sigma²,1e−8), normalize the vector to mean one when possible, clip its entries to [0.05,20], and blend 80% of the old variances with 20% of this vector; renormalize to mean one.

Let p_success be the fraction of offspring whose exact scores beat the old mean score by more than 1e−12. If p_success>0.25, set sigma=min(0.25,1.12·sigma); if p_success<0.08, set sigma=max(5e−4,0.85·sigma); otherwise keep it unchanged. Retain the best exact candidate seen by this restart independently of its changing mean. Stop at the configured generation cap, or after 12 consecutive generations without a restart-best improvement when sigma≤0.002. Return only the restart’s best feasible, exact-scored candidate.

3.8. In run, initialize the global archive from the saved fallback. Scan the start pool and update the archive only for a strict exact improvement greater than 1e−12. Select up to the configured number of restart centers by sorting pool scores ascending, taking the current global best first, then taking score-ranked starts whose maximum absolute distance from already selected centers is at least 1e−3. Run the evolution routine serially from each center, resetting its covariance shape to the SDP-derived initial shape (or the specified identity/tangent shape) and using the seeded generator. Use starting sigmas [0.04,0.09,0.18,0.07] in restart order. Compare every returned restart candidate to the global archive by exact_score; a restart never replaces the fallback merely because its surrogate or population rank changed.

Before returning, project the selected archive vector again, require is_feasible, and recompute exact_score. Compare it with the separately saved fallback score. If projection, validation, or scoring fails, or the candidate is worse than the fallback by more than 1e−12, select the fallback. If fallback recovery itself fails, use and project the constant 0.5 vector. Recompute its exact score. Return a one-dimensional float64 NumPy array, its finite exact score as a Python float, and n as an integer equal to the array length.

4. Search choices and useful variations

Use these complete defaults. Run the SDP only through n=64; retain at most 32 starts and use 12 covariance-rounding samples when available. For n≤64 use lambda=20 offspring per generation, at most 60 generations per restart, and at most 4 restarts. For 65≤n≤128 use lambda=16, 35 generations, and 3 restarts. For 129≤n≤256 use lambda=12, 20 generations, and 2 restarts. For 257≤n≤999 use lambda=8, 12 generations, and 1 restart. Use the 80-step capped-simplex bisection, 1e−12 score-improvement threshold, stated sigma schedule and adaptation, 1e−8 pool deduplication, and 1e−3 restart-center separation. The fallback is always saved independently of pool and restart limits.

Correctness requirements are fixed: preserve runtime n; satisfy both box and mass constraints jointly; include every finite-support lag in the exact score; minimize rather than maximize; use only an SDP solver that supports the PSD formulation; project and exact-score every candidate; and never return a worse candidate than the saved fallback. Never use circular correlation, report t as the answer, or claim a global optimum.

Meaningful resource variations may change the SDP cutoff within 48–80, the rounding sample count within 8–24, and the population budgets within roughly 0.75–1.5 times the defaults while reducing work as n grows. Starting sigma values between 0.02 and 0.20 are practical. The defaults above require no preliminary experiments. Any variation remains seeded, finite, and exact-score-ranked; larger budgets are heuristics, not evidence of a better result.

5. Numerical robustness and memory use

Use float64 throughout. Reject NaN and infinity at input, projection, relaxation-result, covariance, candidate, and score boundaries. The projection brackets a monotone scalar equation, and its residual correction changes only coordinates with available box capacity. If it cannot meet the stated tolerance, discard the proposal. Clamp negative eigenvalues introduced by solver roundoff before taking square roots; if covariance data remain invalid, fall back to P for small n or unit diagonal variances for large n. A solver exception, missing supported solver, non-optimal status, nonfinite output, or failed SDP model disables that stage without disabling the rest of the program.

The dense SDP and full covariance are restricted to n≤64: Y is at most 64×64 and M at most 65×65. At larger n store only O(n) diagonal variances, not a dense covariance, Hessian, lag Jacobian, or lifted quadratic model. Exact scoring stores the 2n−1 correlation entries and uses the required np.correlate operation. Its work is quadratic in n; the population, generation, restart, and start caps bound the number of evaluations up to n=999. Execute everything serially on the allowed one CPU.

All trajectories have finite iteration and restart limits. Nonfinite or infeasible proposals are discarded. The evolving mean may be worse than its best elite, so keep the exact-score archive separately. If no candidate improves the fallback, return the fallback. No result from the SDP or stochastic search is trusted without projection, feasibility validation, and exact rescoring.

6. Runtime safeguards and return contract

The generated program must perform all parsing, parent validation, optimization, candidate checks, exact scoring, and recovery when the harness calls run() with no arguments. Use the pre-imported initial_h_values at runtime when usable; do not copy its entries into source text or redefine the global. Check that the selected n is an integer in [1,999], that every candidate has shape (n,), finite entries, bounds within tolerance, and mass within tolerance, and that the final score is finite.

Implement the authoritative score in program code as max(np.correlate(h, 1−h, mode='full')*(2.0/n)) over all 2n−1 entries. Keep the validated parent-derived fallback and its exact score throughout the search. Accept a candidate only after capped-simplex projection, feasibility checking, and exact rescoring, and retain it only if it improves by more than 1e−12. On any final failure recover to the fallback, or to the constant 0.5 vector if necessary, and recompute the score. The return interface is exactly (h_values, c5_bound, n_points), with h_values a feasible one-dimensional float64 NumPy array, c5_bound its freshly computed exact evaluator score as a Python float, and n_points the matching integer length. The program writes these runtime operations; it does not provide a precomputed vector or score.
